cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-19-christ.summary: At the left the psalmist, armed with spear and shield at the head of his soldiers, appeals to the Christ-Logos, who sits in a globe-mandorla with angels and holds out a bow toward him. Below, the same king brings gold and animals for sacrifice at an altar, while at the right those who 'trust in chariots and horses' are brought down. The drawing pictures the prayer 'the Lord hear thee in the day of trouble'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-19-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

walters:W.432.61R.summary: Christ, in a long grey robe, stands calmly at the centre as a soldier in red seizes him and armed men with spears crowd behind. At the left, a disciple raises his arm to strike, and a fallen man sprawls on the ground before Christ. The miniature accompanies the words 'Cohors ergo et tribunus et ministri Iudaeorum comprehenderunt Iesum et ligaverunt eum' ('Then the band and the captain and officers of the Jews took Jesus and bound him').
facts: The miniature is one of the small Gospel illustrations of John's Passion in an early 16th-century prayer book made in Leiden.
The Walters notes that most of the book's Gospel images are rendered primarily in grisaille, with touches of colour, as here.

walters:W.432.61R.notes: Origin in Leiden and the date 1500–1525 follow the Walters manuscript description (TEI, The Digital Walters). The worklist year (800) was a parsing error for '1st quarter 16th century'. The Walters TEI gives the accompanying text as 'John 1:12-27', evidently a slip for John 18:12–27. The fallen man is presumably Malchus.

feat:uhde-suffer-the-little-children.summary: Christ, in a plain robe, sits in a simple contemporary room where shy village children approach him, some eager, some hanging back. Fritz von Uhde, a former army officer turned painter, brought Christ directly into the everyday world of the poor, and his light-filled, unsentimental naturalism stirred both admiration and controversy.
facts: Uhde's German title, "Lasset die Kindlein zu mir kommen," quotes Luther's translation of Christ's words in the Gospel of Mark.
Uhde's practice of placing Christ among modern working people scandalized some conservative critics, who found it irreverent.
His bright, airy palette shows the influence of Dutch painting and French plein-air artists; Uhde later helped found the Munich Secession.
It was Uhde's first religious painting; it won medals in Berlin, Paris and Munich in 1884 and was shown again at the 1889 Paris exhibition, where Uhde received a Grand Prix.

Q3997714.summary: Christ stands on Mount Tabor in a great oval of white light, arms outstretched in a gesture that foreshadows the Cross, while the heads of Moses and Elijah float beside him. Below, Peter, James and John recoil in wonder, and the Virgin and St. Dominic look on in contemplation. Painted for the cell of a Dominican friar, the serene image was meant to guide quiet prayer rather than to dazzle a crowd.
facts: Fra Angelico and his assistants frescoed each of the friars' cells, each image intended as an aid to meditation; the Transfiguration is among those universally accepted as by his own hand.
The presence of the Virgin and St. Dominic, who were not at the Transfiguration, models the prayerful response the viewer should have.
Fra Angelico was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1982 and named patron of artists in 1984.
Christ's cruciform pose links his glory on the mountain with his coming Passion, as in the Gospel's conversation about his 'departure'.

wga:k/klinger/paintin2.summary: Christ, accompanied by the virtues, enters the sunlit garden of the Greek gods, and the Olympians react with surprise, curiosity and alarm, while Psyche kneels before him. Klinger staged the passing of the classical world before Christianity as a single monumental tableau. Painting, sculpture and frame are fused into a Gesamtkunstwerk several metres wide.
facts: Klinger, a painter, sculptor and printmaker, believed the arts should be united; marble figures and a carved predella form part of the work.

Completed in 1897, it entered the Austrian state collection (now the Belvedere) in 1901, at a time when the artists of the Vienna Secession greatly admired Klinger; since 1938 it has been on long-term loan to Leipzig's Museum der bildenden Künste, where it hangs in the Klinger room.
Klinger is also known for his polychrome Beethoven monument, the centrepiece of the Secession's famous 1902 exhibition.
